tip: Insisto que with the indicative (está) asserts a fact you're sure of. Switch to the subjunctive and it becomes a demand that someone act.
Raiz literally means root. Calling a place or person raiz says it's rootsy and authentic, no frills.
Show de bola literally names a dazzling bit of ball play, a football spectacle now used as all-purpose praise for anything great.
Pão-duro is literally hard bread, and it labels a tightwad too stiff to loosen up and spend.
Manda comes from mandar, which fronts casual speech commands: manda a real (be honest), manda ver (go for it).
Partiu is literally departed, past tense, but it works as let's go: Partiu praia means we're off to the beach.
Dar conta de means to handle or manage something. Deu conta do recado is she pulled off the errand she was handed.
The corda is a wind-up spring, so estar com a corda toda means fully wound up, bursting with energy.
The -ão ending is an augmentative: ligeiro (quick) plus -ão gives ligeirão, a real quick one. It scales up many adjectives.
A menina dos olhos is literally the pupil of the eye, the same body-part image English packs into apple of the eye.
Cara is literally face, but as a word you address someone with it's Brazil's all-purpose dude.
Osso is literally bone, and tá osso means it's tough going, hard as a bone to chew.
Vacilo comes from vacilar, the cognate of vacillate: a slip of hesitation that turns into a careless blunder.
Empurrar com a barriga is literally to push it along with your belly, shoving a task forward instead of actually doing it.
Com o pé na jaca is literally with your foot in the jackfruit, the image for having gone overboard.
Ter o rei na barriga is literally to have the king in your belly, as if pregnant with royalty, so it means acting self-important.
Mãozinha adds the diminutive -inha to mão, a little hand. The tiny form softens the offer of help, a very Brazilian touch.
Com a corda no pescoço is literally a rope around the neck, and it points to money or debt pressure, not just any tight spot.
Com o pé atrás is literally with one foot back, poised to step away, so it means being wary or suspicious.
Dar uma plus a verb-ada makes a quick, casual action: uma segurada (a hold), uma olhada (a look), uma parada (a stop).
Tiro e queda is literally a shot and a fall: one shot and the target drops, so it means a sure thing that can't fail.
Chutou o balde looks like kick the bucket but is a false friend: it means snapping and giving it all up, never dying.
Pano pra manga is literally cloth for a sleeve, plenty of fabric left to work with, so there's much more to the story.
Dar com a língua nos dentes is literally your tongue hitting your teeth, the moment a secret slips out and gets told.
Portuguese can't leave a preposition dangling at the end like English does. Referir-se keeps its a up front: a quem me refiro.
Where English says the fact that he was late, Portuguese uses an infinitive with its own subject: o fato de ele ter se atrasado.
Fora próspera means had been prosperous. This -ra pluperfect is literary; in speech you'd say tinha sido próspera instead.
Pese comes from pesar, to weigh, so em que pese is roughly however it may weigh, a frozen formal formula meaning despite.
After se for a future condition, Portuguese uses the future subjunctive: Se eu obtiver a aprovação means if I get approval.
Boca fechada, a closed mouth, carries the lesson: keep quiet, no flies get in, and you stay out of trouble.
In faz-se mister, mister means necessary and has nothing to do with the English title. It's archaic formal speak for it is required.
Cola comes from colar, literally to glue, but in school slang it means to cheat; a cola is a crib sheet.
Mix with the porcos and you'll end up eating farelo, bran: the proverb warns that bad company rubs off on you.
Gato escaldado, a scalded cat, carries the once bitten, twice shy idea: one bad burn leaves you wary of even harmless cold water.
Embargo here isn't a trade ban. Sem embargo de is a formal legal connective meaning notwithstanding or in spite of.
Em plus a gerund, as in em sendo assim, is literally in being so, a formal Portuguese pattern English never builds.
In Antônio Conselheiro's sertão-and-mar prophecy, virar is the everyday become-verb: virar mar means to turn into sea.
Gonzagão adds the -ão augmentative to Gonzaga, the baião king, giving big Gonzaga, an affectionate size-up Portuguese applies to people.
In far-se-á the pronoun se sits inside the future verb, splitting fará open. This ultra-formal split is written and legal only, never spoken.
Prejuízo usually means loss or harm, not prejudice, which is preconceito. Yet sem prejuízo de is the legal calque of without prejudice to.
